content: Dogs can sometimes carry microorganisms that have the potential to cause illness in humans and other animals. It is essential to wash your hands thoroughly after handling your dog, its food, waste, or any supplies associated with it. Regular veterinary care is crucial to maintain your dog’s health and to prevent the transmission of diseases. Always supervise young children when they are interacting with dogs, even if the dog is a trusted family pet. Dogs can have a profoundly positive impact on their owners' lives. They contribute to the social, emotional, and cognitive development of children, encourage physical activity, and provide companionship. Some dogs are even capable of detecting medical conditions such as impending epileptic seizures or certain types of cancer. Additionally, dogs can help alleviate stress and anxiety. Approximately 38% of households in the United States own at least one dog. However, it is important to note that dogs, regardless of their age, can sometimes harbor harmful pathogens that may cause illnesses ranging from mild skin infections to severe diseases. Diseases Transmitted by Dogs Dogs can transmit a variety of diseases to humans, including but not limited to: Brucellosis Campylobacter infection Capnocytophaga infection Cryptosporidiosis Tapeworm infections Echinococcosis Giardia infection Hookworm infection Leptospirosis Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) Plague Rabies Ringworm Roundworm infection Salmonella infection Sarcoptic mange Tickborne diseases Tularemia Staying Healthy Around Dogs To minimize health risks, always supervise children when they are playing with dogs. Before adopting or purchasing a dog, ensure that the breed and temperament are suitable for your family. Consult with a veterinarian to select a dog that aligns with your lifestyle and needs. Hand Hygiene Wash your hands with soap and running water: After handling dogs, their food, water dishes, or supplies. After contact with dog saliva or feces, even if you used a bag to pick it up. After handling dog food, treats, toys, or bowls. Before eating or drinking. If soap and water are unavailable, use an alcohol-based hand sanitizer containing at least 60% alcohol. For children under five years of age, adults should supervise handwashing to ensure it is done properly. Cleaning Up After Your Dog Dog feces can carry pathogens that may infect humans and other animals. Always pick up and dispose of dog waste properly, even in your own yard. This is especially important in areas where children play. Keeping the environment clean reduces the risk of disease transmission. Preventing Dog Scratches and Bites Dog bites can result in pain, injury, and infections. Approximately 20% of individuals bitten by dogs require medical attention. Dogs may bite when they are scared, nervous, eating, playing, or protecting their toys or puppies. They may also bite if they are unwell and wish to be left alone. To prevent bites: Avoid disturbing a dog while it is eating, sleeping, or caring for puppies. Do not pet a dog that appears to be hiding or seeking solitude. Stop petting a dog if it shows signs of fear, illness, or aggression. If a dog knocks you over, curl into a ball, tuck your head, and cover your ears and neck with your hands. When interacting with unfamiliar dogs: Always ask the owner for permission before petting their dog. Allow the dog to approach you first and remain still to help it feel comfortable. Ensure the dog has seen and sniffed you before attempting to pet it. What to Do If Bitten or Scratched Even minor dog bites or scratches can transmit germs. For minor wounds: Wash the area thoroughly with soap and water. Apply an antibiotic cream. Cover the wound with a clean bandage. For deep wounds: Apply pressure with a clean, dry cloth to stop bleeding. Seek immediate medical attention if the bleeding does not stop or if you feel faint or weak. Consult a healthcare provider if: The wound is deep or serious. The wound shows signs of infection, such as redness, swelling, or fever. You are unsure if the dog has been vaccinated against rabies. It has been more than five years since your last tetanus shot. Report dog bites to your local animal control agency or police department, especially if the dog’s rabies vaccination status is unknown or if the dog appears ill or behaves abnormally. Keeping Your Dog Healthy Maintaining your dog’s health is essential for the well-being of both your pet and your family. Choosing a Dog Before adopting or purchasing a dog, research the breed’s temperament, size, activity level, and care requirements. Ensure the dog’s characteristics align with your family’s lifestyle. Select a dog that appears bright, alert, and playful, with a healthy coat and no signs of illness such as lethargy, diarrhea, abnormal breathing, or discharge from the eyes or nose. Schedule a veterinary visit within a few days to a week after adoption. Housing and Environment Provide a safe, warm, and comfortable environment for your dog. If your dog is housed outdoors, ensure it has shelter to protect it from extreme weather conditions and access to fresh water and food daily. Consider fencing your yard to provide a secure area for your dog to play while protecting it from wild animals and strangers. Avoid tying your dog outside, as this can increase the likelihood of aggressive behavior and is illegal in some areas. Feeding Your Dog Safely Follow food safety guidelines when handling dog food and treats: Avoid feeding dogs in areas where human food is prepared or consumed. Wash your hands after handling dog food or feeding your dog. Store dog food separately from human food. Avoid feeding your dog a raw diet, as raw pet foods can contain harmful bacteria like Salmonella and Listeria. Routine Veterinary Care Schedule regular check-ups with your veterinarian to monitor your dog’s health and prevent infectious diseases. Discuss preventive treatments for fleas, ticks, heartworms, and other parasites. Keep your dog up to date on vaccinations, including rabies, and consult your veterinarian about additional vaccines based on your dog’s lifestyle and exposure risks. Tick Prevention Check your dog for ticks daily, especially after outdoor activities. Remove any ticks promptly and consult your veterinarian about the best tick prevention products for your area. By following these guidelines, you can ensure a safe and healthy relationship with your dog while minimizing health risks for your family.
